The visible slide text identifies the session as "UPS/FORTNA OptiSweep Training - D 1" and includes a date/time stamp of 2026-03-17 13:16 UTC. This establishes the source as a formal training session opening frame rather than an operational screen.

The OCR and artifact retrieval text both indicate the names Mitchel Flynn and Samuel Prescott on the opening slide. The source supports these names as part of session attribution, but does not define their roles, responsibilities, or access levels.

The artifact is tagged as a title slide and intro frame. It contains session-identification text and presenter names, with no visible operational controls, metrics, alarms, or status indicators. This context helps distinguish introductory training content from actual OptiSweep interface content.

The transcript is primarily pre-session conversation about attendee arrival, meetings, hearing each other, Wi-Fi availability, and room comfort. Near the end of the segment, the speaker states, "All right, we'll get started. My name is Mitchell Flynn. This is Akron. We'll be going through this morning's slides." This indicates the segment marks the beginning of a formal training presentation rather than operational system content.

Before the formal start, participants discuss people arriving later, whether attendees can hear each other, lack of Wi-Fi access except "PS Wi-Fi," and room comfort topics such as heater availability and temperature. These details describe the training environment and session logistics rather than OptiSweep system operation.

The available transcript is dominated by casual conversation and meeting logistics. Aside from identifying the session as part of OptiSweep training and noting that morning slides will be reviewed, the segment does not describe system components, HMI screens, alarms, statuses, metrics, or operating concepts in a stable technical way.

The presenter states that the morning session will cover 'just the overview' and explicitly asks, 'So what is Opti Suite?' The slide shown in the segment reads 'Overview What is Optisweep?' This indicates the segment is an introductory overview of OptiSweep rather than detailed operating content.

The presenter says, 'this morning we'll go through just the overview' and 'If you don't know the system,' which frames the material as foundational orientation content. No detailed screens, metrics, alarms, or procedures are presented in this segment.

In a traditional small sort system operators are assigned sections of destinations, approximately 20–25 on a sorter. Parcels divert down the destination and fall into a bag. When the bag becomes full, the operator closes the destination, prints a label, applies the label to the bag, zips the bag, places it on a takeaway belt, and then reopens the chute. The transcript adds that this is slow and involves strenuous up-and-down operator movement.

The OCR text states that in a belted ACB solution, when a destination is full the bin is dropped on a takeaway conveyor. The conveyor moves the packages as a slug down a chute into a bag station, where the user applies a label, zips the bag, and places it on a takeaway belt. The transcript also notes that the belted solution uses conveyor infrastructure and is generally constrained to straight-line layouts, making it complex in certain areas.

FORTNA wanted a more modular and adaptive design that would need little modification to existing sorters. It further states that by utilizing AGVs and tippers, solutions can be scaled and maps can be tailored to existing building sorters. The transcript similarly describes the system as modular and contrasts it with conveyor-based approaches that are more constrained.

The speaker states that OptiSweep software integrates everything so that all connected elements talk and work as a team. The slide shows OptiSweep Software among the core elements and visually associates it with other components including UPS Chat, Geek+ AGVs, hospital controller, sorter, printer, and Aveva HMI.

The slide labeled as an overview of core elements includes UPS Chat, tote tipper or tote tip stations, Geek+ AGVs, hospital controller, OptiSweep Software, sorter, printer, and Aveva HMI. The transcript also references communication with the scan tunnel, tipper, and sorter, and mentions tote tip stations and Geek+ AGVs as part of the environment.

In the transcript, the speaker states that there is a hospital controller for removing and adding totes. The overview slide includes Hospital Controller as one of the core elements in the architecture.

Geek+ AGVs operate over QR codes. The AGVs are directly controlled by Geek+ RMS, which handles all movement and determines the best route from point A to point B. RMS is described as external to the AGV and functions as the robot management system that dictates what the robot needs to do.

The training explains that if the AGV detects an obstacle in front of it, the physical hardware triggers that condition and reports it back to RMS. RMS then generates an alarm code. The alarm is described as visible to personnel viewing the RMS screen, including UPS and others monitoring RMS.

The OCR slide text states that these AGVs have forward collision sensors. It also states that this version of the AGVs is intended to operate in a fenced system. These statements provide safety-related context about the AGV deployment and sensing configuration.

The speaker describes tote racks and notes that operators will see them later in the day. The tote sits on the cylinder, and the slide is labeled as tote racking. The artifact OCR also indicates the design was intended to securely position the tote for parcel impact.

According to the speaker, the tote rack has little feet so that when the tote drops, it is aligned to the center. The speaker emphasizes that the fit is pretty tight, indicating the alignment feature is intended to position the tote accurately within the rack.

The speaker explains that the tote rack has fins on the side that help move packages toward the center if they hit. This describes a passive mechanical centering feature intended to reduce off-center package placement within the tote.

The slide OCR text states that the tote racking was Fortna designed and installed and references a beveled design to securely position the tote for parcel impact. In the spoken explanation, the rack features are described in terms of keeping the tote centered and helping parcels land toward the center.

Each operator station has two tippers. An incoming load from an AGV is clamped by the tipper, the tipping arm actuates to dump contents onto the chute, and the tote is then placed back onto the AGV. The slide presents this as a Fortna R&D design concept for the station.

The source identifies several stable functions of the tipper assembly: it clamps the tote arriving from the AGV, uses actuators to tip the arm, dumps the tote contents onto the chute, and places the tote back onto the AGV. These statements describe the component's role in material transfer rather than an operator procedure.

The tipper station has a self-contained HMI for operation and fault recovery. The transcript also references an HMI in the context of the tipper station. No screen layout, navigation path, or commands are provided in this segment.

The slide explicitly notes that operators are equipped with an E-stop. This indicates emergency stop capability is part of the operator-facing safety provisions at the tipper station. The segment does not provide reset behavior, stop scope, or recovery procedure.

The source describes OptiSweep software as the software that 'integrates everything.' The slide and transcript identify AVEVA as the HMI and Ignition as the OPC server. The same segment also names Chat XLE as the UPS communications endpoint and S-Tunnel as the encrypted or secure channel used for connectivity from the OTNet to the UPS corporate or local UPS network.

Ignition is 'our OPC server.' The speaker also confirms that OPC is a protocol and refers to it as an industry standard protocol. The source further states that Ignition communicates through the tippers through OPC and feeds data to AVEVA because AVEVA can directly integrate with the OPC server.

The OCR slide text explicitly labels 'Aveva - HMI.' The transcript adds that data is fed to AVEVA because AVEVA can directly integrate with the OPC server. This positions AVEVA as the operator-facing HMI layer in the software architecture described in the training segment.

The speaker explains that the system runs through a recurring sort lifecycle. AGVs begin in a shutdown state at specific locations where they charge. During startup, the system takes AGVs from a power cycling state to a staged-for-sort state. During the bulk of the sort, items are sorted and AGVs take full totes to the tippers for bagging. A bag-out cycle then processes locations that still have items in a tote to finish out the sort. Afterward, the system returns to shutdown and AGVs cycle back to chargers.

According to the training discussion, AGVs start in a shutdown state and sit at specific locations where they charge. Startup transitions AGVs from a power cycling state into a staged-for-sort state. At shutdown, AGVs stage and cycle back to the charger. This segment presents these as normal operating states within the sort lifecycle.

During the bulk of the sort, items are actively sorted and AGVs take full totes to the tippers for bagging. The bag-out cycle is described as cycling all locations that still have any items in a tote so the sort can be finished out. This provides a source-grounded distinction between the main sort phase and the completion phase.

In discussion, participants note that state transitions can fail under multiple conditions and that this logic is built into the software. The speaker says the system will indicate faults. Examples mentioned include seeing an AGV waiting to do an exchange during shutdown, or startup delay while the system waits for an AGV on the charger. The segment does not enumerate all failure conditions, but it does establish that transition issues are surfaced by the system.

Before parcels reach the OptiSweep-controlled portion of the system, they are unloaded from trailers in bulk onto a series of belts that lead to sorter induction. As parcels move through this flow, system messaging is triggered and parcel data becomes available. The source states that by the time a parcel is on the sorter, dimensional data is available and there is an indication of where the parcel could be going.

The first message from Chat is triggered as parcels move toward sorter induction. This message includes a tracking ID, dimensions, and package type. The transcript and slide both present this message as the first parcel data event described in the lifecycle.

The slide and transcript describe a fallback condition in which a parcel is seen as unknown inducted if the first message fails. In that case, OptiSweep assigns default dimensions. The transcript also mentions an example default dimension value in discussion, but the stable source-backed concept is the use of default dimensions when the expected message fails.

The OCR text on the slide references weight and dimensions in the context of tote accumulation and software-based fullness determination. It also notes that dimensions are scaled up by software based on package type. The source ties these measurements to the assessment of tote occupancy rather than to a specific operator procedure.

The OCR text on the slide notes that if the first message fails and an unknown item is seen inducted, it is assigned default dimensions by OptiSweep. This indicates a fallback data behavior for inducted parcels when expected upstream message content is missing.

According to the speaker, a parcel has a ZIP code, and UPS internally maintains a mapping file where a ZIP code can map to a single destination or multiple destinations. The transcript also states that this is dynamic and comes from the ASX system. The local system and the order context only know destinations, meaning destination information is the relevant downstream representation discussed in this segment.

The training segment explains that the goal of the exchange is to have one AGV come behind another and move simultaneously together. In the described exchange, an AGV with a full tote moves out into the aisle while an AGV with an empty tote moves into the rack location. The AGV entering the rack lowers its empty tote into the rack. The segment presents this as a speed-focused exchange concept tied to KPI performance.

The segment explicitly mentions thresholds related to the exchange process. It states that staging for an exchange can happen when a tote is immediately full, completely full, or imminently filled. The OCR text also supports the concept that staging can happen when a tote is imminently full or completely full.

After the AGV with the empty tote moves into the rack location and lowers its tote, the segment explains that this AGV then becomes the AGV that will pick up the next tote. The OCR text similarly states that the AGV with no tote becomes the AGV that will pick up the next full tote in that zone. This indicates a role transition in the exchange cycle.

The speaker states that the chute is opened when the AGV moves in, not when it drops a tote. This behavior is described as intentional and tied to strict KPI requirements and the need to speed up exchanges. The segment does not define the KPI numerically, but it clearly associates chute timing with performance expectations.

A full tote sits in the aisle on an AGV and, when it reaches the sorter, Execute assigns a specific tipper. The assignment method is described as round robin across available enabled tippers serviced by the queue. The AGV is then sent to the tipper entrance queue. When the AGV reaches the front of that queue and the tipper becomes available, the AGV is sent to the tipper.

Once the AGV is released from the tipper entrance queue, it travels to the tip location. The source states that the software informs the tipper controller using OPC that the AGV has staged for a tip. This establishes the interface point between OptiSweep software and the tipper controller during the tip staging phase.

The slide and transcript describe the AGV state after a full cycle completes. The tipper informs the software that the AGV is clear to move out. From that point, the AGV can take one of several destinations: return to the sorter, go to the hospital, or go to charge. This is presented as background system behavior in the training material.

The slide and transcript describe the normal return state when the AGV does not go to hospital or charge. In that case, the AGV returns to the sorter entrance queue carrying an empty tote, and that empty tote will be used for the next exchange.

In the discussion, the speaker explains that an AGB may be sent to the hospital when photo sensors cannot see the tote correctly, such as when the tote is pushed back too far or positioned abnormally, or when the mechanism cannot clamp down fully on the tote. The hospital is referenced as a physical area in the layout rather than a continuously manned station.

The speaker states there is usually not a dedicated operator standing at the hospital station. Instead, the supervisor moves back and forth through the area, and personnel at the two closest tipper positions may also keep an eye on the hospital. The station is said to make an annoying noise, which helps draw attention when intervention is needed.

The slide and narration describe the layout design as modular, with separate operational areas connected by a common entrance and exit structure. The stated design principle is that to move from one area to another, an AGB must pass through an exit before entering the next area. This is presented as a general layout concept in the example site design shown.

The slide OCR explicitly lists area names used in the layout: Hospital, SorterSide, Charger, and Tipper. The narration also references hospitals, sorter sides, chargers, and tippers as distinct areas in the modular design. The example shown is described as an older version of the Hazlet layout.

The training segment describes several named areas in the sorter layout. Anything entering the sorter area must first go to the entrance queue. Queue locations are used for AGVs to stage behind for an exchange. Sorter queue locations are where a tote is picked up and moved into the aisle. After an exchange, movement goes to the exit queue before going elsewhere. The segment presents these as core layout concepts for understanding sorter-side flow.

The segment explains that shutdown queues exist in the sorter layout. It states that some shutdown locations are under the rack and that AGVs move to shutdown locations during shutdown. The narration distinguishes locations for AGVs without totes and a location for AGVs with totes. It also notes a special shutdown behavior: if an AGV enters through the entrance during a shutdown state while carrying a tote, it goes to an off-the-end location and then to shutdown.

The segment explains bag out as the condition where the sort is done and all locations must be cleared because load plans and sort destinations change between sorts. It states that every chute is closed whether it contains anything or not, and bag out begins. Any tote with an item in it is exchanged or marked for exchange. The explanation says the process works from back to front, with AGVs going to the farthest area of their zone and then proceeding in sequence to reduce travel time. Once bag out is completed, everything is out of the system and the next sort can start.

The speaker explains that operations may include multiple sorts in a day, such as preload, day sort, and twilight. These sorts do not simply run into each other because they serve different purposes and route volume differently. The segment notes that between sort phases there are transitions, and even in peak season those transitions still exist, though the gap may be smaller. Preload is described as an early morning sort with a specific purpose of creating bags for brown trucks.

The sorter side has zones and compares them to work areas on the manual side. An AGV in a zone only picks up and drops off within that zone. The speaker describes AGV behavior as coming into its zone, checking whether anything needs to be exchanged, and then moving on. The discussion also mentions backfill and that the exchange logic is not very complex and is basically FIFO, while still considering zone conditions.

The speaker explains that 'tipper A&B' are tip locations and that each one has its own tipper queue. Once an AGV is done tipping, it proceeds onward through the modeled flow shown on the slide, which connects the tipper area to hospital-related entrance and exit queues. The slide OCR also shows separate entrance queue labels for tipper A and tipper B as part of the modularized layout.

After the prior stage an AGV goes to the hospital entrance queue first. If the drop-off location is free, it drops off there and then moves to its pickup location. If a tote is present, it picks it up; otherwise it waits for a tote to be picked up. After leaving, it goes to the exit queue. The slide OCR also shows hospital-related labels including entrance queue, dropoff, pickup, tote, and exit queue.

The speaker gives a specific shutdown-state scenario: if an AGV that does not have a tote is removed and another AGV is added, the added AGV goes through the hospital first. The transcript then states it determines that an AGV is missing and goes to the shorter side. This is presented as part of how the system behaves during shutdown-related AGV changes, not as a formal procedure.

The transcript explains that the charger has an entrance queue and tote locations where an AGV drops off its tote while it goes to charge. The speaker states that it does not like to charge with totes on it. After charging is complete, the AGV goes to pick up its tote in a shutdown state example; if some AGVs do not have totes, they do not need to do that. It then proceeds to its exit queue. The slide OCR also shows charger-related labels including chargers, entrance queue, tote, pickup, and exit queue.

The speaker explains that shutdown queues are where AGVs remain while shut down. During startup, AGVs move from shutdown queues into their own zones. The segment notes a four-zone example and says AGVs with totes return and get ready. Shutdown logic also includes cycling AGVs through charging while the system is not actively sorting.

The discussion explicitly says shutdown is something the user chooses from the HMI. This is presented in contrast to the automatic return to running after bag out. The transcript also references “using a Viva HMI” when putting the system into shutdown, indicating the HMI is the operator interface for that state selection.

The speakers explain that the solution is planned for peak, and that some behaviors may make more sense in that context. They mention that entering shutdown sends AGVs to charge, which can slow immediate restart if another run is needed soon. The discussion also references scaling and planning around peak values, including more APBs/sorters/tippers/AGVs as part of system design context.

The speaker explains that users will see buttons that help navigate around the RMS application. The top-right area includes language selection. A sidebar menu may be hidden and can be expanded. Once expanded, the second option is identified as Map Monitor, which is described as the area where users will probably spend most of their time in RMS.

The speaker states that Geek Plus is a Chinese company and that sometimes, when logging in, the default language is Chinese. The language section is described as the third icon from the right in the top-right corner, and it can be clicked to switch the interface to English.

The speaker notes that the sidebar menu is sometimes hidden. A control identified in the explanation as item number three can be clicked to expand the menu. The OCR text also indicates that the menu can be expanded or collapsed.

The speaker says that once the sidebar is expanded, the second option is Map Monitor. The transcript describes it as probably where users will spend most of their time in RMS. The OCR text states that Map Monitor allows users to view the map and AGV movements.

The presenter states that clicking the map overview gives an overview of the system. The map is referenced as the basis for separating the sorter side, charger side, and tipper side. The source indicates this is a visual system layout view rather than a workflow or procedure.

The slide text labels a 'Map Monitor Message Panel' and indicates it is on the right side. The panel content shown in the source includes count of active robots, count of robots charging, a drop down to show AGV faults, count of AGVs disconnected, inspection to view details of fault, locate faulted AGV, and an E-stop the system item.

The OCR text on the training slide explicitly lists 'Count of active Robots' and 'Count of Robots charging' as items in the Map Monitor message panel. These appear to be summary metrics presented in the interface.

The training segment describes the first summary item as the open message panel. It is used when there are pending messages containing active errors or warnings on the system. The panel also provides access to alarm history generated over the past 24 to 48 hours.

The segment explains that one summary point is the active robot count, which indicates how many robots are actively running in the system. Another displayed count shows how many robots are actively charging at the moment.

The training explains that a small drop-down may sometimes be hidden. If there is a current fault that needs to be addressed, it will show there, and opening the drop-down allows the user to see the errors.

The segment defines disconnected AGVs as AGVs that have lost communication from RMS. RMS is described as the application running on the server, while AGVs are on Wi-Fi. The speaker notes that disconnection can happen for multiple reasons, including site Wi-Fi communication loss or an AGV being turned off. The count reflects how many AGVs the RMS thinks are disconnected.

During discussion of disconnected AGVs, the speaker states that shutdown is different from turned off. Shutdown is described as terminology used to define a state of the OptiSweep operation. The speaker advises using turned off rather than shutdown when referring to powering off an AGV.

In this training segment, the presenter describes additional Map Monitor icons that help users understand paths and inspect map objects. The OCR and transcript identify functions including View all AGV active paths, View Station Ids, View Charger Ids, and selection modes for Robot, Container, Cell, and Charger. The left-side panel is described as the place where users choose the object type they want to inspect before clicking items on the map.

The presenter explains that clicking the View all AGV active paths icon causes the map to show all active paths for AGVs. Each path is described as a small blue line that starts from the AGV and ends where the AGV wants to go. This feature is presented as a way to help users understand pathing when receiving calls from different sites.

The training explains that a cell can represent a lane or a station, but stations are special locations. An example is given where an orange-marked item is a station while a light blue or gray item is a cell. Because stations are special, each station has a unique ID. The presenter states that AGVs can be asked to go between stations using these unique IDs and notes that station IDs are important for debugging and identifying problems.

The presenter states that charger IDs exist similarly to station IDs. Clicking the relevant icon shows all chargers in the system with their unique IDs. An example is given that if the system has 10 chargers, there will be 10 unique charger IDs.

The training notes that certain things on the map are clickable, but the map contains multiple object types. To inspect an object, the user must first choose the object type from the left-side panel. The transcript lists robot, container, cell, and charger as the available selection modes. The presenter explains that if a user wants to inspect a robot, they must first click the robot selection icon, with the same concept applying to the other object types.

In the Robot option, a selected robot is shown with a box around it. When a robot is selected, the interface displays robot details. If the detail section is hidden, a small arrow can be used to expand it and show the available detail information about the robot.

The training segment identifies robot ID and location as important details to review after selecting a robot. It also states that the node code is pretty much the cell code for the robot. In the panel, the robot ID may be shown together with a tote identifier, described in the example as tote #96, which is the unique identifier of the tote inducted on the robot.

The segment explains that a robot carrying a tote may be recognized by a small brown box shown on top of the AGV in the display, and the tote appears under the robot ID. If the tote has a question mark before it, this indicates the robot has been removed but the tote has not. If the robot is not carrying any tote, the brown box is not shown and the tote section says layer_1.

Robots have two LEDs on each side and that LED colors indicate robot status. Purple indicates robot disconnected. Blue means robot is in task. Flashing blue means the robot is looking for a label. Green indicates the robot is idle and not in task. Red indicates a fault or low battery.

The source shows a screen or slide labeled "Robot Selection Add and Remove." The visible content is divided into "Add Robot" and "Remove Robot" sections. The add section references entering the corresponding robot ID, clicking "Add," and the system showing that the adding was successful. The remove section references entering the corresponding robot ID or selecting the robot, clicking "Remove," and the system showing that the removal was successful.

For the add action, the source says the system will show that the adding was successful. For the remove action, the source says the system will show that the removal was successful. The source does not specify the exact message text or visual format, only that a success indication is shown.

The slide title text includes 'Robot Selection' and 'Restart Robot'. OCR text shows the screen guidance: 'Enter the corresponding robot Id or select the robot' and 'Click “Restart”'. The screen is presented as part of training content describing how to perform a robot restart from the interface.

OCR text on the slide states: 'The robot will restart (it is at the restart point or on the QR code cell).' This indicates the restart function is described in relation to the robot being located at a restart point or on a QR code cell.

OCR text states: 'After starting, the robot that has been positioned will be displayed on the station map.' This describes a post-restart visualization behavior in the interface, where the robot appears on the map after it has started and been positioned.

In response to a question about who has access, the transcript states that any device connected on the OT network, including a laptop or computer, will have access to the web software application through the IP address. This describes local network-based access to the Geek Plus RMS interface.

To restart a robot, the operator either puts in the ID or selects the robot of interest and presses the restart button on the panel. The OCR slide reinforces this by showing a 'Restart Robot' screen with instructions to enter the corresponding robot ID or select the robot, then click 'Restart'.

The speaker states that if the robot is in the middle of a transaction, it will resume the transaction after restart, and that the task does not get lost for restarts if the robot does not get lost. The segment further states that removal from the system is different: when the robot is removed, it must go through an initialization process, and that is the case where the task is described as 'lost'.

The source explains that when an AGV is in a green state, it is ready to execute but may not currently have a task. In that condition, the operator can use the Go-to function to move the AGV from one point to another. The target can be selected by target code or by clicking a cell on the map and confirming. The slide text states that an AGV not in a task can be sent to any square, and the transcript describes this as a way to avoid physically pushing the AGV.

The transcript gives an example where an AGV is removed and added back, then sent using Go-to to the hospital.
